name: Neutral spine

card.summary: The spine's balanced alignment between postural extremes, used as the reference for standing and lifting posture that looks upright and balanced.
card.note: Experts debate the ideal spinal posture and whether posture causes back pain.

quick.overview:
Neutral spine is the term in medicine and fitness for good posture: the spine aligned between extremes, with gentle inward curves at the neck and lower back and an outward curve in the upper back. A plumb line from the front should divide the body evenly.

For looks, upright alignment shows in a taller, more open standing frame. Core-stability training uses neutral spine as the position to maintain while exercising.
quick.how: People practice holding the alignment while standing, sitting and lifting, and core-stability programs start with controlled neutral-spine awareness before progressing to movement.
quick.risks: Experts still debate optimal spinal posture, and a review found no consensus on whether poor posture causes low back pain.

lead: Neutral spine is the term medicine and fitness use for good posture: the alignment of the body between its postural extremes.[1] Seen from the side, the neck (cervical) and lower back (lumbar) curve inward and the upper back (thoracic) curves outward; seen from the front or back, the 33 vertebrae should appear vertically aligned.[1] It is the reference position for standing posture and for many lifting and core-stability exercises.

For appearance, an upright, balanced stance reads as a taller, more open frame, with shoulders stacked over the hips and the head carried over the torso rather than forward of it. People working on posture, from lifters to those correcting a desk-bound slouch, use neutral spine as the target they are aiming for. In training, core stability is defined as the ability to maintain a stable neutral spine position, and programs teach cues for biomechanically neutral alignment before adding dynamic movement.[2][3][4]

Research attached to the concept is mostly about training and back health rather than looks: reviews and trials of core-stability and stabilization exercise [2][6]. Experts still disagree about the optimal spinal posture, and a systematic review of reviews cited by Wikipedia found no consensus on whether spinal posture causes low back pain.[1]

angle.text: Holding neutral alignment changes how the body is carried, which affects apparent height and shoulder and chest posture.

paras: The spine has three main curves in the side view: the cervical section (C1-C7) curves inward, the thoracic section (T1-T12) curves outward, and the lumbar section (L1-L5) curves inward, with the fused sacrum and coccyx sitting between the pelvic bones.[1] Departures are described as excess curvature (cervical or lumbar lordosis, thoracic kyphosis) or reduced curvature (flat back, lumbar kyphosis), and sideways curvature seen from the front or back is scoliosis.[1] These usually occur in more than one plane at once but are discussed plane by plane.[1]
A neutral pelvis is slightly tilted forward, with the front hip bones just ahead of the pubic symphysis rather than directly above it.[1]

Posture is traditionally assessed with a plumb line. From the front the line should run down the midline and divide the body evenly; from the side it should pass through the ear, the cervical vertebrae, the shoulder joint, the lumbar vertebrae, the hip joint, just behind the kneecap and the foot bones, which is taken to indicate balance between front and back.[1]

Scoliosis is measured with the Cobb angle method, which the Scoliosis Research Society accepted in 1966. Wikipedia notes that normal side-view curvature varies widely between individuals, so sagittal curvatures have not been standardised, and that 2D methods have limits while 3D imaging is not yet reliable enough for clinical reference.[1]

Posture is read socially as well as anatomically. Wikipedia's overview of posture as nonverbal communication reports that an upright spine and raised head are associated with well-being, drooping shoulders and a bowed head with malaise, and that open postures are read as friendly.[8] It also lists a 2018 study in which erect posture was associated with better math scores under stress.[8] Mouth breathing is described as able to push the chin forward and worsen forward head posture.[8]
The appearance chain people describe is aligned spine, then upright stance, then a taller, more open silhouette. Wikipedia's neutral spine article itself does not discuss appearance or height.[1]

A 2005 review describes the core muscles as the bridge between upper and lower limbs and says that stability initially requires maintaining a neutral spine but must progress beyond the neutral zone in a controlled manner, starting with exercises that isolate specific core muscles before complex movements.[3] A 1992 occupational-medicine review defines stabilization training in neutral spine as education in posture and body mechanics combined with exercise for strength, flexibility, endurance and coordination.[6]

A 2008 clinical commentary proposes a three-phase volleyball programme: phase one teaches neutral alignment at low velocity, phase two adds faster multiplanar movements while keeping the spine neutral, and phase three adds sport-specific skills, again with neutral alignment; the authors say prospective research is needed to confirm effectiveness.[4] A 1990 review of exercise and the back advocates an upright posture with minimal forward lean in running.[9]

A 2009 review for dancers notes that most back-pain research has focused on maintaining neutral postures, whereas dancers must learn to move with control through the full range of lumbar extension.[5]

A meta-analysis of randomized trials in chronic low back pain defined core stability as the ability to maintain a stable neutral spine position and compared core stability exercise with general exercise.[2] Wikipedia reports that a systematic review of reviews found no consensus on whether spinal posture or physical exposure causes low back pain, and that experts disagree about the optimal posture, including for sitting.[1] No studies found testing neutral spine specifically as a way to change perceived attractiveness or height.

Neutral spine is a frequent topic in strength-training forums, mostly in relation to squats and deadlifts. In a 2018 T Nation thread, a poster who said he could not brace well with a neutral back and pulled rounded asked which was more dangerous; most replies favoured braced and neutral positions, one citing researcher Stuart McGill, and the thread ended without agreement.[7]

timeline.event: The Scoliosis Research Society accepts the Cobb angle method for measuring spinal curvature.[1]
A review defines stabilization training in neutral spine for back-pain patients.[6]
A review presents core stability as the centrepiece of training, starting from neutral spine.[3]
A three-phase neutral-spine trunk-stabilization programme is proposed for volleyball athletes.[4]
A review for dancers looks at moving beyond neutral spine.[5]
A critical appraisal of a core-stability versus general-exercise meta-analysis appears in the Journal of Athletic Training.[2]

lore.intro: In lifting and posture discussions, neutral spine is treated as the safe and upright reference position, with debate over how rigidly it must be held under load.[7]

claims.claim: Keeping a neutral spine under load is safer than rounding.
claims.believers: Most posters in a 2018 T Nation thread rated braced-and-neutral safest and rounding under load as high risk.[7]
claims.experts: Core-stability literature treats neutral spine as the starting position but says training must progress beyond it in a controlled way.[3] No consensus exists on whether posture causes low back pain.[1]

claims.claim: Neutral spine makes you look taller and more open.
claims.believers: Posture-minded members describe upright alignment as raising apparent height and chest and shoulder position.
claims.experts: Wikipedia's posture overview links upright posture with well-being and open posture with friendliness; no study tests neutral spine on perceived height.[8]

claims.claim: Core-stability training built on neutral spine helps back health.
claims.believers: Programs teach neutral alignment first, then add movement.[4]
claims.experts: A meta-analysis compared core stability with general exercise for chronic low back pain.[2]; the volleyball programme authors say prospective validation is needed.[4]

claims.believers: Plumb-line standards present a single textbook alignment.[1]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes normal sagittal curvature varies widely and experts disagree on optimal posture; dancers are trained to move beyond neutral.[1][5]
